properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Field wish #51 from the dev_storyflow agent sessions (art:dev-storyflow-feedback-2026-09-27, first full session on flo2.io, 2026-09-27 evening), in the reporter's words: "Tool descriptions that match hosted mode: on flo2, say 'omit `approver`; the signed-in person is the approver' instead of 'REQUIRED'." And: "The tool descriptions should say what the hosted server actually expects."

WHAT IS MEASURED. flo2's door rebinds approver: any value but the caller's flo2 contributor id is refused, and an absent one is filled in. It forwards reflow2's descriptions unchanged (185 of 185), and its preamble says neither "omit approver" nor what the caller's id is (flo2 design: fact:root-cause-the-door-rebinds-approver-and-says-so-only-in-its-refusal-2026-09-28). An approver naming the caller's own flo2 id does pass. The class, in reflow2's design, is fact:root-cause-the-served-text-describes-one-deployment-and-a-host-changes-the-rules-under-it-2026-09-28: 8 approver-taking tools and 6 skills tell the agent to name the approver.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN:
(a) THE DOOR REWRITES WHAT IT FORWARDS. flo2 amends the approver description on every tool whose schema carries it, driven by the schema the way its approval rule already is. It already rewrites 4 schemas at that door.
(b) THE DOOR SAYS IT ONCE, in its handshake preamble: "leave approver out, or name yourself, <your contributor id>". Telling the caller its id also makes the served text true as written, since naming yourself passes.
(c) reflow2 TAKES A HOST-DECLARED CONTRACT: a registry flag or handshake field meaning "approvals are bound by the host". reflow2 then changes its own text at the source, and every tool added later is covered.
(d) reflow2 WRITES THE APPROVER TEXT DEPLOYMENT-NEUTRAL: "the Contributor whose word this is; a host that signs its callers in may fill it in and refuse any other name".
(e) A PER-DESIGN LESSON with `steps` on the approver-taking tools. Any design can do this today, and reflow2 appends it to those descriptions. It is cheap, but it is per design, and it is design content standing in for the host's contract.

COST AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside it:
- A description that varies by deployment makes the tool list's fingerprint vary by door. flo2 has recorded that a description change forces people to reconnect.
- reflow2's own contract is deliberate: a host-supplied identity "is never used as an approver" (cap:a-write-is-credited-to-who-it-was-for). Putting flo2's authority policy into reflow2's text, as in (c) or (d), would describe a rule reflow2 does not enforce.
- (b) may be the smallest real fix: the refusal exists because the agent cannot know its own id, not because it named an approver.
- A related gap: the door fills in approver for rejected and superseded too (any status but proposed), which reflow2 does not ask for. It is worth checking before the text says "the signed-in person is the approver".
properties.name: OPEN — should the tool descriptions an agent reads on a hosted door say what that door actually expects (on flo2: "omit `approver`; the signed-in person is the approver"), and whose text changes: the host's, or reflow2's?
properties.rationale: Recorded open because it is a field wish, and because its options put the change in two different products whose contracts deliberately differ (reflow2: approver is always named explicitly; flo2: approver is bound to the sign-in). Which text should change is Anthony's call, and the choice between the host rewriting and reflow2 accepting a host-declared contract is the real question.
